A young participant adds to River of Recovery, a 24-foot community mural created as part of Williams Lake First Nation's National Addictions Awareness Week programming. A painted salmon is one of the images community members added to the Chilcotin River scene in River of Recovery. A 24-foot mural painted during Williams Lake First Nation’s National Addictions Awareness Week will hang at the Nation’s Cwelcwélt Health Station. Titled River of Recovery, the mural depicts the Chilcotin River at Farwell Canyon, where dozens of community members added images and symbols of healing and recovery and tributes to loved ones they’ve lost at Elizabeth Grouse Gymnasium on the closing day on Nov. 6. The youngest contributor to the River of Recovery mural was about five and a half months old. Her mother added a tiny footprint. Several elders in their 80s also contributed. The Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) l Addiction Awareness Week programming took place from Nov. 2 to Nov. 6. The opening day began with a community march and candlelight vigil, and the final day’s event included naloxone training. The local week programming took place ahead of National Addictions Awareness Week, which runs from Nov. 15 to Nov. 21 across Canada. Over the five days, WLFN hosted workshops, community gatherings, wellness services, and recovery activities. 1f8430898597dae8f01640ef53bf1b58.text: Chad Marchand was among the vendors at last Saturday's Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market with his custom hardwood cutting boards. It was everything locally made at the Williams Lake Tourism Discovery Centre on Saturday, Nov. 14 where the annual Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market was held. More than 700 people filtered in to explore 28 vendors set up on all three floors offering a variety of wares. New this year was Chad Marchand of Williams Lake with his custom hardwood cutting boards. The professional forester with BC Timber Sales handcrafts the end grain boards in a small shop in his family’s backyard where they are also sealed with beeswax. “I wanted one for my own brisket making,” Marchand said with a laugh, adding he still doesn’t have one for himself just yet. “Every time one comes out I can’t decide this is the one for me so I just keep on making them.” It has been approximately five to six months that Marchand has started making his unique cutting boards that he typically does after work along his other hobby, gardening. Tourism Discovery Centre operations manager and Williams Lake and District Chamber of Commerce executive assistant Tanya Hutchison called Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market a great way to bring local vendors and showcase their artisan skills with the community. Their products also might not be necessarily found in any other store. Marchand hopes to participate in other upcoming local holiday markets and has already signed up to be part of next year’s Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market.

Williams Lake students looking for something to wear to graduation can try on dresses and suits and take an outfit home for free at Ever After Attire’s Borrowed Magic pop-up. The drop-in event runs from 12 p.m. to 3 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 21, in the Graham Kelsey Room at the Central Cariboo Arts and Culture Centre. Admission is free and no registration is required. Nikki Blodgett, program coordinator for Ever After Attire remembers looking for a graduation dress when she was in high school. “Shopping for a grad dress was so expensive and I wondered how everyone could do it,” Blodgett said. She took over the program from Williams Lake photographer Rick Magnell and has been running it for about a year. Ever After Attire’s lending program is open to graduates in the Williams Lake area regardless of financial circumstances. Blodgett said the collection includes about 125 dresses, along with suits, dress pants, shirts, ties, dress shoes and heels. A change room will be available, and students can bring a friend or parent to help with fittings. Volunteers can also help students choose an outfit or lace up a dress. Ever After Attire said seamstress Dominique Bouchard will be on hand to help with small fixes, such as loose straps or fasteners, and offer advice on alterations. Students who find an outfit they want to borrow can leave their name and phone number and take it home that day. Dresses and suits are due back to Cariboo Corner within two weeks after graduation. Wanda Ranson from Dream Day Bouquet Floral Design will be offering a free floral-themed craft, and Sparkle Booth will provide free photos. Permanent jewellery will also be available for a fee by appointment, Blodgett said. During the provincial election campaign’s home stretch in late October, premier-designate Lorne Doerkson held a boisterous rally in a Surrey warehouse, hitting his major talking points to thunderous approval. One of the biggest applause lines came when he mentioned the B.C. schools initiative called Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity 123. “We are going to get our grades up, and we are going to repeal SOGI!” Doerkson shouted. SOGI 123 is a set of resources provided by an organization called the ARC Foundation to help teachers talk about sexual orientation and gender with students, with the goal being to reduce stigma and bullying. It is sometimes mistakenly referred to as a curriculum and confused with sex education, which it is not. Christy Clark’s B.C. Liberal government created it via a ministerial directive in 2016, and over the past 10 years SOGI-inclusive learning has been threaded into the education system. (Clark sat ringside at Doerkson’s Surrey rally, cheering him on.) As a set of educational resources rather than a law, SOGI 123 is not technically subject to repeal. So what could Doerkson mean in practice when he says he wants to repeal SOGI? And how will schools continue to work to protect gender-diverse students from bullying and harassment? This past summer, the B.C. government ended its partnership with ARC, leading the foundation to wind down operations. In some sense, this means that the province’s schools have already moved beyond SOGI 123. In a news release, then-Conservative Party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay and the party’s education critic at the time, Lynne Block, hailed the termination of the ARC partnership as the “end of SOGI.” According to B.C. c99cecf48a644b68453a76c90064410a.text: Fundraising target set at $3.5M for robotic surgical system for B.C. hospital | Williams Lake Tribune Fundraising target set at $3.5M for robotic surgical system for B.C. hospital Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation wants to raise $3.5 million to bring a da Vinci Surgical System to Nanaimo Regional General Hospital. Various images of the da Vinci Surgical System Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation wants to bring to the hospital in Nanaimo. A non-profit intends to bring the first surgical robotic system to Nanaimo Regional General Hospital for more precise surgeries. In a press release, Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation says it hopes to raise $3.5 million in its 2026/27 winter fundraising drive for the da Vinci Surgical System for use at NRGH – it would be the first robotics program in Nanaimo and the second on Vancouver Island. A “robotic-assisted surgical platform,” the system utilizes a doctor’s hand motions, translating them “into precise, real-time movements of miniaturized instruments inside the body,” according to the press release. “It combines high-definition 3-D visualization, instruments with greater range of motion than the human hand, and advanced features to support highly precise, minimally invasive surgery,” it noted. Robotic-assisted surgery has become the norm for care in hospitals across the continent and affords hospital personnel the ability to “operate with enhanced precision, visualization and control through smaller incisions, including in areas of the body that can be difficult to reach using conventional surgical instruments.” At first, the da Vinci Surgical System will be utilized for procedures such as those for kidneys, colorectal and prostates, with intention to add ear-nose-throat surgery and gynecology, in the future. Supreme Court judge dismissed a defamation lawsuit brought forward by the former mayor of Quesnel’s wife against a city councillor over comments made during a 2024 council meeting. In a decision published on Nov. 10, Justice Tindale ruled that Quesnel Coun. Laurey-Anne Roodenburg’s statements about Pat Morton’s distribution of a book questioning the findings surrounding residential schools were protected under the Protection of Public Participation Act. Morton, the wife of former Quesnel Mayor Ron Paull, filed the lawsuit following comments Roodenburg made during a March 19, 2024, council meeting. According to the court document, the controversy began after Morton distributed copies of _Grave Error: How the Media Misled Us (and the Truth about Residential Schools),_ which she had purchased in February 2024. On March 19, 2024, Lhtako Dene Nation sent a letter to the mayor and council expressing concern about the book, saying it questioned the existence of residential schools and whether cultural genocide had occurred. The letter called on council to reaffirm its Memorandum of Understanding with the Nation and offered to have Elders who attended residential schools share first-hand knowledge of their experiences with council. According to the court document, during the meeting in March, Paull identified his wife as the person distributing the book and said he had not read it. Roodenburg, who was serving as the city’s Indigenous Liaison at the time, criticized Morton’s actions, saying they showed a lack of respect for the mayor’s position and were causing harm to members of First Nations communities. “I respect the fact that people have the right to their own opinions, but what I don’t see here is the respect that your wife has shown you in your role as mayor of this community,” Roodenburg said at the time, according to the court document. “We know that what has happened reflects not only on you, but on council and on our community as a whole. NDP calls for opposition to Quebecor’s Telus takeover bid The Telus Park building on 64 Avenue in Surrey, pictured on Nov. 18, 2026. Interim B.C. NDP Leader Jennifer Whiteside is calling on the incoming government to oppose Quebecor’s $31-billion bid to take over Telus, warning it would reduce competition and could lead to higher prices for British Columbians. “Consolidating two major national telecommunications players will inevitably reduce competition in our market, leading to fewer choices, diminished service quality, and higher monthly bills for families and small businesses,” Whiteside said in a letter addressed to incoming premier Lorne Doerkson. Telus is B.C. based, while Quebecor is headquartered in Montreal. Both companies compete in B.C.’s budget cell-phone market: Telus owns Public Mobile, and Quebecor owns Freedom Mobile. In addition to reducing competition, Whiteside says the shift to East Coast ownership would be bad for B.C.’s economy. Telus is headquartered in Vancouver and has multiple new office buildings under construction. “For decades, Telus has been a cornerstone of British Columbia’s technology and telecommunications sector,” she said. “The prospect of an out-of-province acquisition raises serious concerns for working families, businesses, and our provincial economy.” The takeover bid, which offers cash and shares, would still need regulatory approval. Quebecor argues it would create a “strong pan-Canadian competitor” to compete with other national providers and foreign competitors. Doerkson responded to Whiteside’s letter by saying he wants to ensure British Columbians have choice, competitive prices and reliable cell service. He also wants local jobs preserved. “There are legitimate questions raised by a change in ownership and must be fully considered as part of any approval process,” he said in a written statement. The Lake City Broncos fall basketball program drew players ages 10 to 17, with U14 and U17 girls team and U13, U15, and U17 boys team. The Lake City Broncos recognized players and thanked their youth coaches at the fall awards night on Nov. 12. Each team handed out three awards. The Lake City Broncos U17 girls reached the final and U14 girls picked up a win on their first trip to Vancouver area as an age group. The Lake City Broncos have wrapped up their biggest fall season yet, fielding five travel teams and sending each one to the Vancouver area to compete. The Williams Lake program drew players ages 10 to 17, with U14 and U17 girls’ teams and U13, U15, and U17 boys’ teams, said coach Travis Nystoruk. Nystoruk said all five teams competed even though fall is typically the Broncos’ shorter season, with fewer tournaments to choose from than in spring. The Broncos travelled to Kelowna, Kamloops and the Vancouver area during the season. Their early trips included a late-September tournament hosted by GW Hoops in Kelowna. In October, the U15 and U17 boys travelled to Langley and Surrey for the DRIVE Fall Classic. The U15 boys reached the silver division final, losing by two points, while the U17 boys finished in a three-way tie for second in their round-robin pool. Nystoruk said the U15 boys had been training with the program for several years and its run to the silver division final showed how far it had come against teams from the Vancouver area. At the Remembrance Day Jamboree, the U17 girls reached the final and the U14 girls picked up a win on their first trip to the Vancouver area as an age group. 449503945dfae9c26e6fbcadc4384558.text: Doerkson lays out immediate priorities, explains B.C. cabinet picks | Williams Lake Tribune Doerkson lays out immediate priorities, explains B.C. cabinet picks B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson speaks to media following the swearing in of his cabinet in Victoria on Nov. 20, 2026. Premier Lorne Doerkson plans to hit the ground running on several campaign pledges, including implementing a promised tax cut as soon as Jan. 1. Doerkson laid out his agenda and explained some of his cabinet choices at his first press conference as premier, shortly after Lt.-Gov. Wendy Cocchia swore him in on Friday, Nov. 20. He said Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity resources in schools, an anti-bullying program known as SOGI 123, will be done away with immediately. However, Doerkson has still not explained how this will work in practice. The new government also plans a comprehensive review of the province’s finances, which new Finance Minister Peter Milobar says will begin in the coming weeks. Other thorny issues like his plans to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act will need to wait until the legislature convenes in the spring. “I’m absolutely committed to repealing DRIPA because it hasn’t solved our problems,” he said. The promised tax cut was a signature campaign promise for Doerkson. But without a fall legislative session, the new government can’t pass the necessary bill before the new year. Doerkson said he hopes to implement the tax changes in the spring legislative session, and backdate it to Jan. 1. The proposal, which the Conservative Party laid out in its campaign platform, is to increase the personal provincial income tax exemption from $13,216 to more than $32,000, providing an effective tax credit of $1,000 for everyone earning that amount or more. This only fully benefits those who earn at least $32,000 per year. People earning less get a smaller benefit, and those without income get nothing. e4126ca92dc2df001fbf9f2c564e589c.text: The Okanagan Falls branch of the Royal Canadian Legion has temporarily shut down, according to a letter shared to the organization’s social media on Nov. 19. According to the letter, BC/Yukon Command of the Royal Canadian Legion has suspended Branch #227’s bylaws and powers, stood down its current executive, and appointed two trustees to act on its behalf. The letter is signed by BC/Yukon president Robert Underhill. The Penticton Western News contacted the BC/Yukon Command on Nov. 19, but has not yet received a reply with additional information. “Despite the support and direction provided during Trusteeship Level 1, ongoing concerns remain regarding the Branch’s financial and operational management, governance and compliance with Legion policies and procedures,” reads the letter. “As these matters have not been sufficiently addressed, additional oversight is necessary to help bring the branch back into compliance and strengthen its overall operations.” This is the second B.C. branch to be placed under trusteeship, following Maple Ridge in September. The Maple Ridge Legion, Branch #88, is the largest in Canada with almost 5,000 members. The letter that was issued to Maple Ridge contains almost the same text as the letter issued to Okanagan Falls, including encouraging the members to continue to remain engaged and support the Branch while it is under trusteeship. More than a decade ago, Penticton Legion Branch #40 was placed under trusteeship for over three years, from 2012 to 2015. Premier Lorne Doerkson is continuing to appoint his MLAs to key roles, with the latest being his caucus leadership team. Canada’s defence minister has asked for a review of the country’s cadet program funding after concerns about cuts and pauses. National Defence Minister David McGuinty said Friday (Nov. 20) that his ministry has heard the concerns raised by cadets, families and communities across Canada about changes to planned activities. He said he will ensure the cadet community is kept informed as the review progresses. “We know how much this program means to young Canadians and the important role it plays in developing leadership, confidence, and a commitment to service.” McGuinty’s statement comes after days of news stories surrounding the state of the cadet and junior Canadian ranger programs amid budget constraints. The Ottawa Citizen first reported a pause for the program, citing an internal document. Some media outlets then reported suspensions or cancellations of cadet meetings. The Department of National Defence issued a statement Wednesday saying that spending was being reassessed and “adjustments” would be required for some planned activities. The department clarified the next day that the core cadet program is not changing, specifically that “adjustments are being made to specific additional activities outside of the core weekly programming.” McGuinty’s statement says the full budget for the cadets this year is $265 million, which is an increase from last year and previous years. “That investment reflects our strong commitment to the program. There will be no changes to core weekly programming.” He also noted that the 2026 Spring Economic Update announced $250 million over five years, starting in 2026–27, to expand Canada’s skilled trades training capacity through the Canadian Armed Forces and that included a $27-million increase for cadets this year. District of Barriere Mayor Rob Kerslake is seeking to spark a conversation about how infrastructure is funded in municipalities, and is pushing for change in the municipal finance system. The mayor of Barriere is looking to spark a conversation about precarious grant programs and stir up change in the municipal funding system in light of daunting critical infrastructure costs facing his town in the coming years. Mayor Rob Kerslake of the District of Barriere remarked that the infrastructure funding gap is not a new topic. “It’s been around for a while,” he said. “What we’re finding in Barriere is, as we dive deeper into our asset management, it tells a story that’s not so great. We have multi-million dollar projects that we have to fund, and you know, for a small town with 1,000 ratepayers, (it’s) near impossible.” A primary pillar of Kerslake’s concern is the precarity of relying on grants to fund such projects. In an attempt to address the issue, he brought a resolution to the Southern Interior Local Government Association (SILGA) convention this year to advocate for new revenue streams for municipalities. The resolution was endorsed by the Union of B.C. Municipalities (UBCM) and is listed in its 2026 Resolutions Book. It points to “significant infrastructure deficits” among local governments across B.C., noting that many are unable to meet needs through property taxes alone. The endorsed resolution calls on UBCM to advocate for the province of B.C. and the federal government to establish a revenue-sharing model that allocates a portion of PST and GST revenues collected within municipal boundaries and electoral areas to go directly back to local governments. 913d64cddffda182b8cbdf77e98d1efa.text: Attorney General Niki Sharma scrums with media at the Union of B.C. Municipalities convention in Vancouver on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. B.C.’s former attorney general is calling on the incoming Conservative government to continue to support Criminal Code changes for AI accountability as further disturbing details of the Tumbler Ridge shooter’s ChatGPT account have been revealed. Niki Sharma said in a statement Thursday (Nov. 19) that AI regulation and accountability are needed after American magazine Mother Jones released its latest story in a five-part investigative series into mass shooters and their use of AI chatbots. The Nov. 19 article further details Jesse Van Rootselaar’s chat logs with ChatGPT in the lead-up to the Feb. 10 mass shooting. “That is why I launched the lawsuit against Sam Altman and OpenAI and why I wrote to the federal government asking for stronger criminal laws that create a clear path to human and corporate accountability for the actions of AI.” Sharma called on premier-designate Lorne Doerkson to confirm that his government supports Criminal Code changes for AI accountability and strong AI regulation, and that it will see the provincial government’s lawsuit through. Doerkson will be sworn in as premier on Friday, along with his cabinet, when a new attorney general will be selected. The B.C. government – then under the NDP – had filed a lawsuit in California against OpenAI in connection with its failure to notify law enforcement of threats on its platform before the mass shooting and for designing an “unsafe product.” OpenAI is seeking to have it moved to a British Columbia court. Today In BC has reached out to the Conservative Party of B.C. for comment. Nechako Lakes MLA-elect Diane Black told media in the B.C. legislature ahead of the swearing-in that “anything that can be done is being done.” Eight people were killed in the northeastern B.C. community of Tumbler Ridge on Feb. 10 when the shooter killed her mother and 11-year-old brother

3d204b9df8f418d1e9893caa8b2b5e8d.text: Bear injures 16-year-old in B.C. town after finding food in residential garage | Williams Lake Tribune Bear injures 16-year-old in B.C. town after finding food in residential garage A black bear sow eating berries at the summit of Mount Revelstoke National Park on Oct. 4, 2025. Police and B.C. conservation officers have confirmed that a black bear was destroyed last Saturday in Revelstoke, B.C., after finding food in an open garage and injuring a boy. The Conservation Officer Service (COS) confirmed with Black Press Media that the bear entered a residential garage in the Arrow Heights neighbourhood on Nov. 14. “Unaware that a bear was inside, a male youth approached the garage and attempted to close the access door,” it said in a statement. “The bear made contact with the youth, resulting in injuries.” With its nearest office being in Salmon Arm, the COS couldn’t attend the scene promptly and asked Revelstoke RCMP to respond. Officers from the detachment arrived to the property and found the bear still in the garage guarding non-natural food sources. Staff Sgt. Chris Dodds told Black Press Media the bear had already injured the 16-year-old boy by the time police were called. “In consultation with the BC Conservation Officer Service, the RCMP dispatched the bear due to public safety concerns,” the COS said. “The victim received medical attention for non-life threatening injuries.” Dodds said the COS eventually attended the scene as well to remove the destroyed bear, and is responsible for following up on the incident. He noted that RCMP was “acting on behalf of the conservation service” and receives numerous human-bear conflict calls every year. “We’ve had lots of bear complaints, right?” Dodds said. “There are attractants in neighbourhoods that they are attracted to.” He added that it’s not unusual for bears to still be visiting town this late in the fall — “it’s no different than any other year.” Kait Nicol, executive director of the Revelstoke Bear Aware Society,

e80bad78e6f0e9befa8a102fb9f50241.text: CNC Dental Clinic offers affordable care while supporting student learning. The College of New Caledonia (CNC) is inviting adults and children to access affordable dental hygiene services through its student-run clinic in Prince George. According to a press release by CNC, the clinic is accepting patients now and will operate until the end of April 2027. Services include dental X-rays and cleaning for a one-time fee of $50 for adults and $25 for children under 18. Patients may require more than one appointment depending on their dental health needs, but the fee remains the same regardless of the number of visits. “Regular dental care is an important part of maintaining overall health, but we recognize that cost can be a barrier for many individuals and families,” Diane Horita, Dental Hygiene Faculty and DS program coordinator at CNC, said. “Our clinic provides an opportunity for people to access affordable care while helping our students develop the clinical skills and confidence they need to become successful dental hygiene professionals. We especially welcome patients who haven’t had a dental appointment in a long time, as these experiences provide important learning opportunities for our students.” CNC also reminds potential patients that appointments take longer than those at a traditional clinic, as services are provided by students under faculty supervision. Patients should expect each visit to last between an hour and a half and three hours, and some treatments may require multiple visits.
